Anyone looking at him might have thought Nemesis had stolen the shield of Pallas and shown him the Gorgon’s head. He appeared petrified, his sorrowful face as still as marble. Until now he had enjoyed the refined, luxurious existence of a wealthy young aristocrat, a life made exquisite by its freedom from sordid worries and its charming, boyish carelessness. For the first time, he understood the dreadful mystery of Destiny and the terrifying meaning of Doom.

How insane and monstrous it all seemed! Could some appalling secret of sin, some blood-red mark of crime, be inscribed on his hand in symbols unreadable to him but plain to someone else? Was escape impossible? Were human beings merely chess pieces moved by an invisible power, pots shaped at the potter’s whim for honor or disgrace? His reason rebelled, yet he felt a tragedy looming above him, as though he had suddenly been ordered to shoulder an unbearable weight. How fortunate actors were. They could decide whether to appear in a tragedy or a comedy, whether to suffer or celebrate, to laugh or weep. Real life offered no such choice. Most men and women were compelled to perform roles for which they had no talent. Our Guildensterns played Hamlet, while our Hamlets were forced to joke like Prince Hal. The world was a stage, but the casting was poor.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers came into the room. He flinched at the sight of Lord Arthur, and his coarse, fat face turned a greenish yellow. Their eyes met. For a moment neither spoke.

“The Duchess left a glove here, Lord Arthur, and asked me to fetch it,” Mr. Podgers said at last. “Ah, there it is on the sofa! Good evening.”

“Mr. Podgers, I must insist that you answer the question I’m about to ask directly.”

“Some other time, Lord Arthur. The Duchess is waiting anxiously. I’m afraid I must leave.”

“You are not leaving. The Duchess is in no hurry.”

“One shouldn’t keep ladies waiting, Lord Arthur,” said Mr. Podgers with his sickly smile. “The fair sex does tend to grow impatient.”

Lord Arthur’s finely shaped lips curled with irritated contempt. At that moment the poor Duchess seemed of very little consequence to him. He crossed the room to Mr. Podgers and held out his hand.

“Tell me what you saw in it,” he said. “Tell me the truth. I have to know. I am no child.”

The little man’s body was disproportionately broad, giving his whole figure a thoroughly ridiculous roundness. Naturally, his feet were completely hidden, although something suspiciously hornlike occasionally poked through a tear in the bottom of the basket—or, more accurately, the top of the hat. His hands were enormous. His hair, extremely gray, was gathered into a queue behind him. His nose was astonishingly long, crooked, and inflamed; his eyes were large, bright, and keen. His cheeks and chin, though lined with age, were broad and swollen into folds. Yet nowhere on his head could one detect even the suggestion of an ear. This peculiar little gentleman wore a loose coat of sky-blue satin, with matching tight breeches secured at the knees by silver buckles. His waistcoat was made of some brilliant yellow fabric, and a white taffeta cap sat jauntily on one side of his head. To complete the outfit, a blood-red silk handkerchief wrapped his neck and descended delicately onto his chest in a fantastical bow of extraordinary proportions.

Having descended, as I have already said, to within about a hundred feet of the ground, the little old gentleman was suddenly overcome by alarm and seemed unwilling to come any closer to solid earth. He therefore lifted a canvas sack with considerable difficulty and scattered some sand from it, immediately bringing his descent to a halt. Then, in a hurried, agitated fashion, he drew a large morocco-leather wallet from a side pocket of his coat. He weighed it suspiciously in his hand and stared at it in considerable surprise, evidently astonished by its heaviness. Finally he opened it and extracted an enormous letter, sealed with red wax and carefully tied with red tape. He dropped it directly at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent to pick it up. At that moment, however, the balloonist, still deeply unsettled and apparently having no further business to keep him in Rotterdam, began busily preparing to depart. To rise again he needed to throw off some ballast. Without bothering to empty them, he tossed out half a dozen sacks one after another. Most unfortunately, every single sack struck the burgomaster on the back, rolling him over and over no fewer than twenty-one times before the eyes of every man in Rotterdam. It should not be imagined, however, that the great Underduk allowed such insolence from the little old man to go unpunished.

Many years ago I became close friends with a man named William Legrand. He came from an old Huguenot family and had once possessed a fortune, but a succession of misfortunes had left him poor. To escape the humiliation of his losses, he abandoned New Orleans, his ancestral city, and settled on Sullivan’s Island, near Charleston, South Carolina.

It is a remarkable island, made almost entirely of sea sand, about three miles long and nowhere more than a quarter of a mile wide. A barely visible creek separates it from the mainland, seeping through a wilderness of reeds and mud much frequented by marsh hens. As one might expect, vegetation is sparse, or at least stunted. There are no large trees. Near the western tip, where Fort Moultrie stands beside a few wretched wooden buildings occupied in summer by people fleeing Charleston’s dust and fever, the bristling palmetto does grow. Apart from that western point and a strip of firm white beach along the seaward shore, however, the entire island is covered by dense sweet myrtle, the shrub so highly valued by English gardeners. Here it often reaches fifteen or twenty feet, creating an almost impassable thicket and loading the air with fragrance.

Deep within this thicket, near the island’s more distant eastern end, Legrand had built himself a small hut. He was living there when I first met him entirely by chance. Our acquaintance soon developed into friendship, for much about this recluse inspired interest and respect. I found him well educated and exceptionally intelligent, though distrustful of humanity and prone to difficult changes of mood, alternating between enthusiasm and gloom. He owned many books but seldom opened them. His principal diversions were shooting and fishing, or wandering along the beach and through the myrtles in search of shells and insect specimens. His insect collection might have made Swammerdamm envious. On these expeditions he was generally accompanied by an elderly Black man named Jupiter. Jupiter had been freed from slavery before the family’s financial reverses, yet neither threats nor promises could persuade him to surrender what he regarded as his right to follow his young “Massa Will” wherever he went. It is quite possible that Legrand’s relatives, believing his mind somewhat unstable, had encouraged this stubborn devotion in Jupiter so that someone would watch over and protect the wanderer.
